title: Shloka 88
subtitle: Sunlight into the heart, and four ways of standing next to Śiva

namas.translation: The darkness lodged in a devotee's heart breaks apart before her, as night gives way to an unbroken stream of sunbeams.

namas.translation: The shape in which Śiva becomes visible is no other than she.
Wherever her attention falls, wellbeing follows, for making things auspicious is her very act.

commentary.meaning: The two lines of this verse are built to opposite specifications. The first is a single compound sixteen syllables long, dense with aspirated consonants, describing one sustained action: the darkness lodged inside the hearts of those devoted to her is broken open by her as by an unbroken stream of the sun's rays. The second line is four short names in a row, every one of them beginning with the same word. What makes the second line more than a chime is that the relation between her and Śiva changes at each step. First he is her messenger, sent on her errand. Then he is her worshipper, offering her what others offer him. Then he is not a separate party at all, since she is the form in which he is seen. And in the fourth name śiva has stopped being anybody's name and gone back to being the adjective it started as — auspicious, benign — so that she is simply the one who makes things well. The line begins with the god as a subordinate and ends with the god dissolved into an ordinary Sanskrit word for kindness.
commentary.history:
The long first name needs unpacking element by element, and it should be said at the outset that the printed texts do not entirely agree on how to divide it. Some read bhakta-hārda, others bhaktā-hārda with the alternative stem āhārda; the sense is the same either way, since hārda and āhārda both derive from hṛd, heart, and mean what belongs to or is lodged in the heart. Tamas is darkness, and in the Sāṃkhya vocabulary the hymn was using two verses earlier it is also the name of the third constituent of nature, the one responsible for heaviness, dullness and obstruction. Bheda, from √bhid, to split, is a breaking apart rather than a dispersal — the darkness is cleft, not merely thinned. Bhānumat, possessed of rays, is a standard word for the sun; bhānu by itself is a ray; and santati, from sam-√tan, to stretch out together, is an unbroken continuity, the same root that gives tantra its sense of something stretched on a loom. The compound therefore says: she is the continuous stream of rays of the ray-possessing one, which splits the heart-lodged darkness of the devoted.

The choice of santati is the interesting part. A single blaze would have made the point about darkness more dramatically, and Sanskrit has plenty of words for a flash. What santati adds is duration and seamlessness. Sunlight is not an event; it is a condition that does not stop arriving. The image is of a room that is lit because the sun has not gone away, which is a different account of how ignorance is removed than the one implied by sudden illumination.

With the second line the hymn arrives at the name that carries a story. Śivadūtī, she whose messenger is Śiva, records an episode from the Devī Māhātmya. In the war against Śumbha and Niśumbha the Goddess needs an envoy sent to the demon kings, and she asks Śiva to go. He goes. When he returns, having delivered her terms, she declares that because she has made Śiva her messenger she will be known in the world by this name. The Devī Māhātmya is careful to make it her declaration rather than a narrator's aside: the name is one she takes for herself on the strength of what she has just been able to ask of him. In the same chapter Śivadūtī also appears as a distinct figure, the fierce power that issues from Caṇḍikā's own body and joins the śaktis of the male gods on the battlefield, so the name has both a narrative and an iconographic life.

Śivārādhyā continues the reversal in a quieter grammar. Ārādhyā is a gerundive from ā-√rādh, to propitiate or please: she who is to be worshipped, with Śiva in the instrumental as the one who must do it. The Saundaryalaharī opens with exactly this claim and draws the conclusion the tantric traditions want from it — that if she is worshipped by Hari, Hara and Brahmā, then a human being's praise is presumptuous unless some merit has already been accumulated. It is worth registering how systematically this hymn inverts the ordinary hierarchy. In most of the surrounding religious literature Śiva is the one addressed; here he is successively the errand-runner, the devotee, and finally the image.

Śivamūrtiḥ is read two ways and the commentators do not settle it. Mūrti, from a root meaning to become solid or congeal, is a form that has taken on definite shape, and hence the ordinary word for a consecrated image. On the first reading the compound is possessive of Śiva — she is his embodied form, the shape in which the formless one becomes available — which fits the sequence perfectly, since it moves the relation past envoy and worshipper into identity. On the second reading śiva is the adjective and the name means one whose form is auspiciousness. Nothing in the grammar decides between them, and the second reading has the advantage of preparing the fourth name.

Because in śivaṅkarī the word has certainly reverted to its adjectival sense. In the oldest layer of the language śiva is not a proper noun at all but an adjective — kindly, gracious, favourable — used of Rudra as a propitiatory address, on the widespread principle that a dangerous power is best spoken to by its mildest attribute. Only later does the euphemism harden into the name of a god. Śivaṅkarī, she who makes what is auspicious, belongs to a small class of Sanskrit compounds in which the accusative ending of the first member is preserved inside the word instead of being dropped — the grammarians call the retained syllable the mum augment, and the same pattern gives priyaṃvada, one who speaks pleasantly, and vaśaṃkara, one who brings under control. The preserved case-ending keeps the verbal force alive: this is not a name for a benign lady but for someone actively doing something to something.
commentary.practice:
The first line is one name and must be recited on one breath, which is the difficulty of the verse. It is also the most heavily aspirated line in this stretch of the hymn: bhakta, bheda, bhānumad, bhānu — four labial aspirates, plus the bh already inside the first syllable. Each bh is a single letter, b with breath forced through the release, and it is quite distinct from the unaspirated b. English speakers usually produce something close to the aspirated version by accident and the unaspirated one only with effort, so the risk in this line is the opposite of the usual one: not too little breath but a slack, indistinct b that could be either.

Two sandhis inside the compound are worth seeing, since they explain spellings that otherwise look arbitrary. Tamas ends in s, which before the voiced bh of bheda becomes o: tamas plus bheda gives tamobheda. And bhānumat ends in an unvoiced t, which before the same voiced consonant becomes d: bhānumat plus bhānu gives bhānumadbhānu. Both changes are the language doing what mouths do anyway, voicing a consonant before a voiced one, and once a reciter recognises the pattern a great many compound spellings in this hymn stop needing to be memorised.

The second line is easy to say and easy to miscount, for the same reason. Four names, each opening with śiva, and nothing but the endings to tell them apart. Fix them by the sequence of relations rather than by sound: messenger, worshipper, form, maker. The ś of śiva is palatal, made with the blade of the tongue near the hard palate, closer to the sh of sheep than to the s of see, and it should be the same sound all four times.

Śivārādhyā contains a join that swallows a vowel. The elements are śiva and ārādhyā, and a short a followed by a long ā produces a single long ā, so the word has four syllables and not five. In śivaṅkarī the nasal written ṅ is the guttural nasal, the ng of sing, and it is there because the following consonant is the guttural k; the tongue makes one closure at the back of the mouth for both sounds rather than two.

For archanā the four short names take three different endings, which makes the line a useful exercise. Śivadūtyai and śivamūrtyai and śivaṅkaryai all shorten a final ī or i into y before the ending, while śivārādhyāyai, being an ā-stem, takes the full -āyai. The long first name gives bhaktāhārdatamobhedabhānumadbhānusantatyai, which is worth attempting once slowly if only to feel how far a Sanskrit compound can be extended without ceasing to be a single word.

What the verse asks of the person chanting is contained in the first line's choice of image. The darkness it names is specifically located — hārda, in the heart, and belonging to bhaktas, to those who are already devoted, not to unbelievers or enemies. The hymn is not describing the enlightenment of the world. It is describing something inside the person reciting, and it does not promise that the darkness will be gone after this verse. Sunlight is continuous or it is nothing.

crossReferences.translation: Out of compassion for those very people, I, standing within their own being, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
crossReferences.relevance: The same three elements as the long name — darkness, its removal, and a light source — with one instructive difference. The Gītā's image is a lamp, brought and lit, standing inside the person. The hymn's is sunlight, which is not brought anywhere and cannot be lit or extinguished. Both agree that the darkness is interior and that the removal is done by somebody else.

crossReferences.deva: शिवः शक्त्या युक्तो यदि भवति शक्तः प्रभवितुं न चेदेवं देवो न खलु कुशलः स्पन्दितुमपि । अतस्त्वामाराध्यां हरिहरविरिञ्चादिभिरपि प्रणन्तुं स्तोतुं वा कथमकृतपुण्यः प्रभवति ॥
crossReferences.iast: śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavituṃ na cedevaṃ devo na khalu kuśalaḥ spanditumapi | atastvāmārādhyāṃ hariharaviriñcādibhirapi praṇantuṃ stotuṃ vā kathamakṛtapuṇyaḥ prabhavati ||
crossReferences.translation: If Śiva is joined with Śakti he is able to act; if he is not, the god is not competent so much as to stir. This being so, how should one who has done no meritorious deeds be capable of bowing to you or praising you — you who are to be worshipped even by Hari, Hara and Brahmā?
crossReferences.relevance: The opening verse of the Saundaryalaharī states the premise that this line of the sahasranāma spells out in four steps, and it uses the same word: ārādhyā, to be worshipped, with Hara — Śiva — named among those who must do the worshipping. It also supplies the reasoning behind śivamūrtiḥ, since a god who cannot stir without her is not a separate agent standing beside her.

references.title: Devī-Māhātmya: The Crystallization of the Goddess Tradition
references.author: Thomas B. Coburn (Motilal Banarsidass, 1984)
references.note: A word-by-word study of the text's vocabulary and sources, including where its epithets come from and what they meant before it used them. The place to go for the Śivadūtī episode and for the observation that the Goddess names herself in that scene rather than being named.

references.title: Saundaryalaharī (Devanagari with Roman transliteration)
references.author: Śṛṅgeri Śāradā Pīṭham
references.note: The first verse, quoted above, is the single most cited statement of the doctrine behind this line of the hymn, and reading the next four or five verses after it shows how the poem develops the claim rather than leaving it as an epigram.

references.title: A Sanskrit Grammar for Students
references.author: Arthur A. Macdonell (Oxford, 3rd ed. 1927)
references.note: Short, cheap, and still the best first grammar in English. The sections on compounds explain the type that śivaṅkarī belongs to, where an accusative ending survives inside the word, and the chapters on consonant sandhi cover both the changes visible in the long first name.

references.title: Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma Stotram
references.author: M. S. Subbulakshmi
references.note: The recording by which most people in South India know this text, and the one that has effectively fixed the standard recitation tempo. Useful for this verse in particular: listen to how she manages the sixteen-syllable first line without breaking it, and how she keeps the four śiva- names distinct without slowing down.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: The entry for śiva runs through the adjective before it reaches the god, which is the historically correct order and the one this verse's last two names depend on. Compare the entry for mūrti, where the sense of congealing or taking solid shape is still visible under the later meaning of a temple image.
